claim: The Tg(fli1aep:ERK-KTR-Clover) transgenic zebrafish line was generated using Gateway cloning and transgenesis.
source: The Tg(fli1aep:ERK-KTR-Clover)uq39bh transgenic line (referred to as Tg(fli1aep:EKC)/EC-EKC in this study) was generated for this study using Gateway cloning and transgenesis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the method used to generate the transgenic line in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Blood vessel development was unaffected in Tg(fli1aep:EKC) transgenic embryos and larvae.
source: Blood vessel development was unaffected in Tg(fli1aep:EKC) transgenic embryos and larvae (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1B-E showing normal vessel development.

claim: Transgenic adults displayed no adverse morphological features and were fertile.
source: Furthermore, transgenic adults displayed no adverse morphological features and were fertile (data not shown), indicating that EKC does not inhibit Erk-signalling in vivo, or cause developmental phenotypes, consistent with previous findings (Mayr et al., 2018; De Simone et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the observation about adult transgenic fish and cites previous studies showing similar findings.

claim: EKC does not inhibit Erk-signalling in vivo or cause developmental phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, transgenic adults displayed no adverse morphological features and were fertile (data not shown), indicating that EKC does not inhibit Erk-signalling in vivo, or cause developmental phenotypes, consistent with previous findings (Mayr et al., 2018; De Simone et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the observation of normal development and cites previous studies.

claim: ISV tip ECs in developing intersegmental vessels have high Erk activity.
source: Tip ECs in developing intersegmental vessels (ISVs) have been shown to have high Erk activity (Costa et al., 2016; Nagasawa-Masuda and Terai, 2016; Shin et al., 2016a), and we observed nuclear depleted EKC localisation in leading angiogenic ISV cells including at the level of the dorsal longitudinal anastomotic vessel (DLAV) in DMSO-treated embryos (Figure 1F–F'',I).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and presents their own observations in Figure 1.

claim: Treatment with SL327 or SU5416 resulted in nuclear enriched EKC localisation in ISV ECs, indicating inactive Erk-signalling.
source: In contrast, ISV ECs of embryos treated with either SL327 or SU5416 had nuclear enriched EKC localisation, indicating inactive Erk-signalling (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental results shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The Tg(fli1aep:EKC) transgenic line enables quantification of Erk activity in developing ECs.
source: Therefore, we confirmed that the Tg(fli1aep:EKC) (hereafter EC-EKC) transgenic line enables quantification of Erk activity in developing ECs.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the validation experiments.

claim: Sprouting ISV ECs display high Erk activity at 22 hpf.
source: We examined 22 hpf embryos and indeed observed that sprouting ISV ECs display high Erk activity based upon EKC localisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: ISV tip cells had higher Erk activity than adjacent DA 'stalk' ECs.
source: We assessed the ratio of nuclear EKC/H2B-mCherry intensity in double transgenic EC-EKC;Tg(fli1a:H2B:mCherry) embryos and found that the ISV tip cells had higher Erk activity than adjacent DA 'stalk' ECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A'' and C).
evidence: The manuscript describes quantification results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear EKC intensity alone is sufficient to compare Erk-signalling between ECs.
source: Next, we investigated whether nuclear EKC intensity alone was sufficient to compare Erk-signalling between ECs. The ratio of nuclear EKC intensity of the sprouting ISV tip cell and the adjacent DA 'stalk' EC clearly showed higher signalling in tip cells and was consistent with EKC/H2B-mCherry measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes validation of the quantification method.

claim: Migrating ECs had higher Erk activity than non-migrating ECs.
source: We found that migrating ECs had higher Erk activity than non-migrating ECs, irrespective of their tip or stalk cell location in an ISV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation between EC migration and Erk activity.

claim: EC Erk activity correlates with cell migratory state based on nuclear ellipticity.
source: This is consistent with previous studies of Vegfa/Kdr/Kdrl/Erk-signalling in zebrafish ISVs (Yokota et al., 2015; Costa et al., 2016; Nagasawa-Masuda and Terai, 2016; Shin et al., 2016a) and confirms a strong correlation between ISV EC motility and EC Erk-signalling.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and confirms the correlation.

claim: ISV tip ECs displayed nuclear enriched EKC localisation during cell division.
source: High-speed live-imaging of ISV tip ECs revealed nuclear enriched EKC localisation during cell division (Figure 2A–C), which was maintained until cytokinesis (Figure 2B, Video 1) but may reflect nuclear membrane breakdown rather than altered cellular signalling.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from live-imaging shown in Figure 2 and Video 1.

claim: Daughter ECs in the tip position progressively increased their Erk activity following cell division, while stalk daughter cells remained nuclear enriched.
source: Subsequently, daughter ECs in the tip position progressively increased their Erk activity, while ECs in the trailing stalk daughter position remained nuclear enriched, showing asymmetric Erk-signalling activity rapidly following cell division (Figure 2B–I, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the dynamic changes in Erk activity post-division.

claim: Tip cells consistently increased their Erk activity relative to stalk cells in a progressive manner with the most dramatic asymmetry observed ~21 min post-cytokinesis.
source: This revealed that tip cells consistently increased their Erk activity relative to stalk cells in a progressive manner with the most dramatic asymmetry observed ~21 min post-cytokinesis (Figure 2J,K, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes quantitative analysis of Erk activity dynamics.

claim: Vessel wounding in 4 dpf larvae results in highly reproducible Vegfa/Kdr/Kdrl signalling-dependent vessel regeneration.
source: We chose this model because vessel wounding in 4 days post-fertilisation (dpf) larvae results in highly reproducible Vegfa/Kdr/Kdrl signalling-dependent vessel regeneration (Gurevich et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing the vessel regeneration model.

claim: Cell wounding induces ERK-signalling in vitro and in vivo in other settings.
source: Importantly, cell wounding induces ERK-signalling in vitro and in vivo in other settings (Matsubayashi et al., 2004; Li et al., 2013; Hiratsuka et al., 2015; Aoki et al., 2017; Mayr et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies showing ERK activation upon wounding.

claim: The majority of ISV ECs in mature vessels have low basal Erk-signalling.
source: EKC localisation in the majority of ISV ECs indicated low basal Erk-signalling in ECs of mature vessels (Figure 3D,D',F,F',H,I, Videos 2–5).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from imaging of unablated control vessels.

claim: Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs immediately increased upon vessel wounding.
source: Upon vessel wounding, Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs immediately increased (Figure 3E,E',H,I, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes the immediate response to vessel wounding.

claim: Erk activity in ECs of ISVs adjacent to the ablated ISV rapidly increased upon vessel wounding.
source: Surprisingly, Erk activity in ECs of ISVs located adjacent to the ablated ISV (termed adjacent ISV) also rapidly increased (Figure 3G,G',H,I, Videos 3 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes the unexpected finding of Erk activation in adjacent vessels.

claim: The level of Erk activation in ablated and adjacent vessels was comparable by 15 min post-ablation.
source: Although the activation of Erk-signalling in adjacent ISV ECs was slower than that in ablated ISV ECs, the level of Erk activation in ablated and adjacent vessels was comparable by 15 min post-ablation (mpa, green dotted line) and consistent up to 22 mpa (Figure 3I).
evidence: The manuscript describes quantitative comparison of Erk activity over time.

claim: Both venous and arterial ECs equally showed Erk activation 15 mpa in ablated ISVs post-vessel wounding.
source: Both venous and arterial ECs equally showed Erk activation 15 mpa in ablated ISVs post-vessel wounding, suggesting that both venous and arterial ECs are able to rapidly activate Erk-signalling (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of Erk activation in different EC types.

claim: The activation of Erk-signalling was largely limited to the wounded and immediately adjacent ISVs.
source: We found that the activation of Erk-signalling was largely limited to the wounded and immediately adjacent ISVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes spatial analysis of Erk activation.

claim: Macrophage recruitment to the wound was minimal at 15 mpa.
source: As previously reported (Gurevich et al., 2018), macrophage recruitment to the wound was minimal at 15 mpa, while robust macrophage recruitment was observed 3 hr post-ablation (hpa), suggesting that macrophages may not contribute to rapid Erk activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and presents their own observations.

claim: Depletion of macrophages led to a quantifiable but mild reduction in normal vessel regeneration measured at 24 hpa.
source: We found that depletion of macrophages led to a quantifiable but mild reduction in normal vessel regeneration measured at 24 hpa in this model (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of macrophage depletion on vessel regeneration.

claim: Rapid EC Erk activation post-wounding was unaffected upon macrophage depletion.
source: The rapid EC Erk activation post-wounding was unaffected upon macrophage depletion (Figure 3K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2K–V').
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of macrophage depletion experiments.

claim: Erk activation in both ablated and adjacent ISV ECs 15 mpa was blocked in larvae treated with SL327.
source: Erk activation in both ablated and adjacent ISV ECs 15 mpa was blocked in larvae treated with SL327, indicating that it requires upstream Mek activation (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–M').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of MEK inhibition on Erk activation.

claim: Treatment with SU5416 and AV951 did not impair the rapid Erk activation at 15 mpa.
source: However, treatment with two independent and validated VEGFR inhibitors, SU5416 (Figure 1H–I) and AV951 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C), did not impair the rapid Erk activation at 15 mpa (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 3O–Z').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of VEGFR inhibition on rapid Erk activation.

claim: At 15 mpa, Erk activation in both ablated and adjacent ISV ECs is induced independently of either macrophages or Vegfr-signalling.
source: Therefore, at 15 mpa, Erk activation in both ablated and adjacent ISV ECs is induced independently of either macrophages or Vegfr-signalling, suggesting an initial response to vessel wounding that has not been previously examined.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Erk activity was maintained until 30 mpa in adjacent ISV ECs, but then gradually decreased and returned to non-ablated control levels by 1 hpa.
source: Erk activity was maintained until 30 mpa in adjacent ISV ECs, but then gradually decreased and returned to non-ablated control levels by 1 hpa (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the time-course of Erk activity in adjacent vessels.

claim: High Erk activity was maintained for the duration in ablated ISV ECs.
source: By contrast, high Erk activity was maintained for the duration in ablated ISV ECs (Figure 4A,A',C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes sustained Erk activity in wounded vessels.

claim: Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs was high at 3 hpa, while ECs in adjacent ISVs were at non-ablated control level.
source: Similar to the time-course analysis, Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs was high at 3 hpa, while ECs in adjacent ISVs were at non-ablated control level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–N).
evidence: The manuscript describes Erk activity at 3 hpa in different vessel types.

claim: An initial activation of Erk-signalling in cells surrounding a puncture wound was only transient.
source: This confirmed that an initial activation of Erk-signalling in cells surrounding the puncture wound was only transient (Video 6) and, in this case, was progressively lost even in cells at the immediate site of the wound, unlike in regenerating vessels.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from Video 6 showing transient Erk activation in muscle and skin cells.

claim: Adjacent tissue ablation resulted in rapid activation of Erk-signalling in ISV ECs.
source: Similar to vessel ablation, this adjacent tissue ablation resulted in rapid activation of Erk-signalling in ISV ECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of control ablation on Erk activity.

claim: Erk activity in ECs following control ablation decreased to non-ablated control levels by 3 hpa.
source: Erk activity in these ECs decreased to non-ablated control levels by 3 hpa (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the time-course of Erk activity following control ablation.

claim: Erk-signalling is immediately activated in muscle, skin epithelial and ECs upon injury, but only regenerating vessels retain this high activity at 3 hpa upon vessel wounding.
source: Therefore, Erk-signalling is immediately activated in muscle, skin epithelial and ECs upon injury, but only regenerating vessels retain this high activity at 3 hpa upon vessel wounding.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the comparison of different wound types.

claim: Treatment with SL327 inhibited Erk activation at 3 hpa.
source: Treatment with SL327 inhibited Erk activation at 3 hpa, as did treatment with the Vegfr inhibitor SU5416 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F',I–J').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of MEK and VEGFR inhibition on sustained Erk activity.

claim: kdrl crispants displayed reduced Erk activity in EC-EKC measurements compared with ISV ablation control larvae at 3 hpa.
source: 3 hpa F0 crispant larvae displayed reduced Erk activity in EC-EKC measurements compared with ISV ablation control larvae (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–T').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of kdrl knockout on Erk activity.

claim: kdrl crispants displayed a mild reduction in Erk activity, likely due to compensation from other Vegfrs, such as Kdr, and/or Flt4.
source: Unlike drug-treated larvae, kdrl crispants displayed a mild reduction in Erk activity, likely due to compensation from other Vegfrs, such as Kdr, and/or Flt4 (zebrafish orthologue of VEGFR3) (Covassin et al., 2006; Shin et al., 2016b).
evidence: The manuscript explains the partial effect of kdrl knockout and cites studies on VEGFR compensation.

claim: Vegfr-/Mek-signalling is required for sustained high Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs at 3 hpa.
source: Overall, these genetic and pharmacological approaches indicate that Vegfr-/Mek-signalling is required for sustained high Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs at 3 hpa.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Inhibition of Vegfr- or Erk-signalling completely blocked all ongoing vessel regeneration.
source: We observed that inhibition of Vegfr- or Erk-signalling completely blocked all ongoing vessel regeneration (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1U–X).
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional consequence of signaling inhibition.

claim: There was no difference in EC-EKC activation at 3 hpa in the absence of macrophages.
source: Finally, we found no difference in EC-EKC activation at 3 hpa in the absence of macrophages, suggesting that macrophages play a modulatory role in vessel regeneration and are not the sole source of Vegfs in this laser ablation model (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of macrophage depletion on sustained Erk activity.

claim: Treatment with SU5416 at 10 μM blocked ongoing Erk activation.
source: Interestingly, we noted that while treatment with SU5416 at 10 μM blocked ongoing Erk activation (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J'), treatment with the same inhibitor at a lower dose of 4 μM did not completely block Erk activity (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H').
evidence: The manuscript describes dose-dependent effects of VEGFR inhibition.

claim: Erk-signalling in the first, second, and third ISV ECs from the wound was activated 3 hpa in control larvae.
source: Erk-signalling in the first, second, and third ISV ECs from the wound was activated 3 hpa in control larvae, while treatment with 10 μM SU5416 inhibited signalling in ECs located in all of these positions (Figure 5E,G,H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D',I–J').
evidence: The manuscript describes spatial analysis of Erk activity and drug effects.

claim: With 4 μM SU5416, the closest cell to the wound site still displayed Erk activity, as did the second cell, but the third cell was inhibited.
source: However, with the intermediate dose of 4 μM SU5416, while the closest cell to the wound site still displayed Erk activity, as did the second cell from the wound site, the third and farthest cells from the wounded sites were now inhibited (Figure 5F,H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H').
evidence: The manuscript describes position-dependent sensitivity to VEGFR inhibition.

claim: There is a gradient of Vegfr/Erk-signalling activity in the ablated ISV ECs resulting in higher Vegfr/Erk activity in ECs closer to the wounded site.
source: These results suggest that there is a gradient of Vegfr/Erk-signalling activity in the ablated ISV ECs resulting in higher Vegfr/Erk activity in ECs closer to the wounded site, which can only be inhibited with SU5416 at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript infers a signaling gradient based on dose-response data.

claim: There is a graded activation of Erk at 3 hpa based on cell position relative to the wound.
source: To test this, we examined the EC-EKC levels relative to cell position and directly confirmed this graded activation at 3 hpa (Figure 5I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–M').
evidence: The manuscript describes direct measurement of the signaling gradient.

claim: During the ongoing response to vessel wounding, Vegfr-signalling is crucial and drives a positionally graded signalling response to regulate regenerating vessels.
source: Together, these analyses confirm that during the ongoing response to vessel wounding, Vegfr-signalling is crucial and drives a positionally graded signalling response to regulate regenerating vessels.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the spatial analysis of Erk activity.

claim: Activated by ATP released by damaged cells, Ca2+ signalling is one of the first intra-cellular mechanisms to be activated post-wounding in many cell types.
source: Activated by ATP released by damaged cells, Ca2+ signalling is one of the first intra-cellular mechanisms to be activated post-wounding in many cell types (reviewed in detail in Ghilardi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a review on Ca2+ signaling in wound response.

claim: Mechanical injury of blood vessels rapidly activates Ca2+ signalling in neighbouring endothelial cells in excised rat aorta.
source: Accordingly, mechanical injury of blood vessels has been shown in situ to rapidly activate Ca2+ signalling in neighbouring endothelial cells in excised rat aorta (Berra-Romani et al., 2008; Berra-Romani et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing Ca2+ activation in injured vessels.

claim: Ca2+ signalling activates Erk-signalling in endothelial cells downstream of the Vegfa/Vegfr2 signalling pathway.
source: Although Ca2+ signalling activates Erk-signalling in endothelial cells downstream of the Vegfa/Vegfr2 signalling pathway (Koch and Claesson-Welsh, 2012; Moccia et al., 2012), Ca2+ signalling alone can also activate Erk-signalling (Xiao et al., 2011; Handly et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the relationship between Ca2+ and Erk signaling.

claim: ISVs in non-ablated 4 dpf larvae did not show Ca2+ signalling, indicating low Ca2+ activity in stable ISVs.
source: ISVs in non-ablated 4 dpf larvae did not show Ca2+ signalling, indicating low Ca2+ activity in stable ISVs (Figure 6B, Video 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from control larvae.

claim: Ablated ISV ECs showed a rapid pulse of active Ca2+ signalling at 5 mpa, which progressively decreased and returned to the level of the surrounding tissue.
source: In contrast, ablated ISV ECs showed a rapid pulse of active Ca2+ signalling at 5 mpa, which progressively decreased and returned to the level of the surrounding tissue (Figure 6A,B, Video 8).
evidence: The manuscript describes Ca2+ dynamics in wounded vessels.

claim: Active Ca2+ signalling was not observed in adjacent ISVs.
source: Active Ca2+ signalling was not observed in adjacent ISVs (Figure 6A,B, Video 8).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial specificity of Ca2+ activation.

claim: Nifedipine treatment did not inhibit Erk-signalling activation in adjacent ISV ECs at 15 mpa.
source: Nifedipine treatment did not inhibit Erk-signalling activation in adjacent ISV ECs resulting in similar Erk activity as DMSO-treated larvae 15 mpa (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B',G–J').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of Ca2+ inhibition on adjacent vessels.

claim: Erk activation in ablated ISV ECs was significantly reduced by Nifedipine treatment compared to DMSO-treated larvae.
source: However, Erk activation in ablated ISV ECs (where we observed the GCaMP signal above) was significantly reduced when compared to DMSO-treated larvae (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F').
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of Ca2+ inhibition on wounded vessels.

claim: The Nifedipine effect was reproduced using Amlodipine, an alternative Ca2+ signalling inhibitor.
source: This was reproduced in an independent experiment using Amlodipine, an alternative Ca2+ signalling inhibitor (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1K–T').
evidence: The manuscript describes validation with a second Ca2+ inhibitor.

claim: Ca2+ signalling plays a crucial role upstream of Erk in the wound response.
source: This indicates not only that Ca2+ signalling plays a crucial role upstream of Erk in the wound response, but also that the response is differentially regulated in ablated compared with adjacent vessels, indicative of additional underlying signalling complexity.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the Ca2+ inhibition experiments.

claim: Activation of Erk-signalling in ablated ISV ECs 3 hpa was not inhibited by Nifedipine.
source: Activation of Erk-signalling in ablated ISV ECs 3 hpa was not inhibited by Nifedipine (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–G').
evidence: The manuscript describes the time-dependent role of Ca2+ signaling.

claim: Inhibition of Ca2+ signalling immediately following wounding between 0 and 30 mpa had no impact on later Erk-signalling at 3 hpa.
source: Inhibition of Ca2+ signalling immediately following wounding between 0 and 30 mpa also had no impact on later Erk-signalling at 3 hpa (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2H–N').
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal specificity of Ca2+ requirement.

claim: Ca2+ signalling is required for rapid Erk activation, but not for maintaining Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs.
source: Thus, Ca2+ signalling is required for rapid Erk activation, but not for maintaining Erk activity in ablated ISV ECs.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the temporal analysis of Ca2+ inhibition.

claim: Ca2+ signalling was highest in the ECs closest to the wounded site.
source: In the analysis of Ca2+ signalling following vessel wounding, we noted that this transient pulse of Ca2+ signalling was highest in the ECs closest to the wounded site (Video 8).
evidence: The manuscript describes spatial analysis of Ca2+ signaling.

claim: Erk-signalling in ECs proximal to the wounded site (first and second positioned ECs) activated first, followed by ECs farther away from the wounded site.
source: Quantitative analysis based on multiple movies (including Video 3) showed that Erk-signalling in ECs proximal to the wounded site (first and second positioned ECs) activated first, followed by ECs farther away from the wounded site (third, fourth, and fifth ECs) (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript describes sequential activation of Erk signaling.

claim: The ECs proximal to the ablation site showed the highest magnitude of Erk activation, and this difference reduced as ECs were positioned farther from the ablation site.
source: Quantitatively, the ECs proximal to the ablation site (first and second positioned ECs) showed the highest magnitude of difference from control, and this difference reduced as ECs were positioned farther from the ablation site (Figure 6H).
evidence: The manuscript describes quantitative analysis of the spatial gradient.

claim: Like the initial burst in Ca2+ signalling post-vessel wounding, Erk-signalling is activated progressively in ECs closest to the wounded site first, followed by those farther away.
source: This shows that like the initial burst in Ca2+ signalling post-vessel wounding, Erk-signalling is activated progressively in ECs closest to the wounded site first, followed by those farther away.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion comparing Ca2+ and Erk dynamics.

claim: ERK-signalling is a downstream target for pathways essential for development including VEGFA/VEGFR2, EGF/EGFR, and FGF/FGFR pathways.
source: ERK-signalling is a downstream target for a number of pathways essential for development (including VEGFA/VEGFR2, EGF/EGFR, and FGF/FGFR pathways) and plays a central role in organ development by promoting proliferation, growth, migration, and differentiation (Hogan and Schulte-Merker, 2017; Lavoie et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites reviews on ERK signaling in development.

claim: The EC-EKC model revealed a very rapid post-cell division signalling asymmetry, confirming previous work based on static imaging.
source: In the context of tip-cell proliferation in angiogenesis, we revealed a very rapid post-cell division signalling asymmetry, confirming a previous work based on static imaging (Costa et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and confirms its findings with dynamic imaging.

claim: This study revealed a two-step mechanism for Erk-signalling activation post-vessel wounding that involves an immediate and ongoing signalling response.
source: In regenerative angiogenesis, we revealed a two-step mechanism for Erk-signalling activation post-vessel wounding that involves an immediate and ongoing signalling response that progressively limits Erk-signalling to vessels that are regenerating.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Studies in zebrafish and Xenopus have demonstrated rapid Erk activation in epithelial cells upon local wounding, which subsides relatively quickly (within 1 hpa) as tissue repair progresses.
source: Studies in zebrafish and Xenopus have demonstrated rapid Erk activation in epithelial cells upon local wounding, which subsides relatively quickly (within 1 hpa) as tissue repair progresses (Li et al., 2013; Mayr et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on Erk activation in wound healing.

claim: There is a common, initial, rapid Erk-signalling response immediately post-wounding in many different cell types and tissues.
source: This suggests a common, initial, rapid Erk-signalling response immediately post-wounding in many different cell types and tissues – as if cells adjacent to a wound are rapidly primed to respond.
evidence: The manuscript infers a general wound response mechanism based on their findings.

claim: In the vasculature, initial rapid Erk signaling returned to pre-ablation levels by 1 hpa, while Erk activity was maintained for a longer timeframe only in the wounded vessels.
source: However, in the vasculature, this signalling returned to pre-ablation levels by 1 hpa, while Erk activity was maintained for a longer timeframe only in the wounded vessels.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics specific to vasculature.

claim: The ongoing, later signaling was maintained through Vegfr activity, likely stimulated in part by Vegfa secreted from macrophages.
source: This ongoing, later signalling was maintained through Vegfr activity, likely stimulated in part by Vegfa secreted from macrophages (Gurevich et al., 2018), and our data suggests other local sources of Vegfs (see Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and adds their own interpretation.

claim: The difference in Erk-signalling dynamics between wounded and unwounded vessels represents an initial priming of the wounded tissue that is replaced over time with sustained vascular Erk-signalling essential in the regenerative response.
source: Thus, Erk-signalling dynamics between wounded (ablated) and unwounded (adjacent) vessels differed significantly. We suggest this difference represents an initial priming of the wounded tissue (the rapid Erk response) that is replaced over time with sustained vascular Erk-signalling that is essential in the regenerative response.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an interpretation of the two-phase response.

claim: Ca2+ signalling is required for Erk activation in ablated ISV ECs.
source: Using both quantitative live-imaging and pharmacological inhibition, we found that Ca2+ signalling is required for Erk activation in ablated ISV ECs.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on experimental results.

claim: Ca2+-dependent Erk-signalling is activated progressively from cells closest to the wound to cells farther away.
source: Taking advantage of the high spatial and temporal resolution in our model, we found that Ca2+-dependent Erk-signalling is activated progressively from cells closest to the wound to cells farther away.
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial dynamics of Ca2+-dependent Erk activation.

claim: The progressive activation may be consistent with a wave of Ca2+ signalling through the wounded vessel.
source: This may be consistent with a wave of Ca2+ signalling through the wounded vessel.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the mechanism of progressive activation.

claim: Activation of Erk-signalling at 2 mpa in wounded epithelial cells in Xenopus promotes actomyosin contraction and wound closure.
source: Activation of Erk-signalling at 2 mpa in wounded epithelial cells in Xenopus promotes actomyosin contraction and wound closure (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the function of rapid Erk activation.

claim: Rapid Ca2+ signalling-mediated Erk activation in the wounded vessel may ensure efficient wound closure in ablated ISVs.
source: Therefore, rapid Ca2+ signalling-mediated Erk activation in the wounded vessel may ensure efficient wound closure in ablated ISVs.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional role for the rapid response.

claim: EC Ca2+ signalling is likely influenced by the activity of either transient receptor potential (TRP) channels or P2X receptors (P2X4 or P2X7).
source: At a molecular mechanistic level, it seems likely that EC Ca2+ signalling is influenced by the activity of either transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Smani et al., 2018) or P2X receptors (P2X4 or P2X7) (Surprenant and North, 2009), which are active in ECs and can influence angiogenesis, cytoskeletal remodelling, and vascular permeability.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on Ca2+ channels and speculates on mechanisms.

claim: There was no evidence that Ca2+ signalling influenced the broader, rapid Erk-signalling response in unwounded but adjacent vasculature.
source: We found no evidence that Ca2+ signalling influenced the broader, rapid Erk-signalling response in unwounded but adjacent vasculature.
evidence: The manuscript states the lack of Ca2+ involvement in adjacent vessels.

claim: Altered tissue tension associated with tissue ablation may contribute to the broader Erk-signalling mechanism, as it has been shown to modulate ERK-signalling in some contexts.
source: One interesting candidate to contribute to this broader mechanism is altered tissue tension associated with the tissue ablation, which had been shown in some contexts to modulate ERK-signalling (Rosenfeldt and Grinnell, 2000; Hirata et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on mechanical regulation of ERK and proposes a mechanism.

claim: Vessel wounding was not required for rapid Erk activation – tissue wounding in between ISVs alone activated Erk-signalling in surrounding ECs.
source: Perhaps consistent with this idea, we did not identify a mechanism required for rapid Erk activation in adjacent ISV ECs and vessel wounding was not required – tissue wounding in between ISVs alone activated Erk-signalling in surrounding ECs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the non-specific nature of the initial response.

claim: Rapid Erk activation in ECs upon wounding seems likely to potentiate these ECs to more rapidly respond to external growth factors such as Vegfa upon the later activation of the inflammatory response.
source: Nevertheless, rapid Erk activation in ECs upon wounding seems likely to potentiate these ECs to more rapidly respond to external growth factors such as Vegfa upon the later activation of the inflammatory response and initiation of sustained regenerative angiogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional role for the initial priming response.
